title: Epitaxial single T centres in silicon-on-insulator
authors: Christian H. Christiansen, Kasper H. Nielsen, Alisha Nanwani, Sebastiano Guaraldo, E. Laurits Piehorsch, Arnulf J. Snedker-Nielsen, Magnus L. Madsen, David R. Gongora, Emanuele Brusaschi, Rodrigo A. Thomas, Ian Farrer, D. Hieu Nguyen, Georgios Kountouris, Beñat M. d. A. Jokisch, Mohammad Khalifa, Claudia Piccinini, Mathias Ø. Augustesen, Hugo Laurell, Kokeb B. Benti, Maria S. Gonzalez, Amedeo Carbone, Elvedin Memisevic, Sangeeth Kallatt, Mark K. Svendsen, Marianne E. Bathen, Lasse Vines, Peter Granum, Peter Krogstrup, Stefano Paesani
abstract: Spin-photon interfaces based on silicon quantum emitters offer a scalable platform for quantum computing and networking. However, achieving coherent photon emission remains a primary challenge due to stringent material quality requirements. To overcome this, we utilise high-purity molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) to epitaxially incorporate single T centres in silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers. We demonstrate single T-centre emission coupled to a nanophotonic waveguide and observe significant suppression of homogeneous broadening, yielding optical linewidths as narrow as 30 MHz using natural silicon for crystal growth. These results establish epitaxial T centres as a robust foundation for coherent spin-photon interfaces in silicon quantum photonics.
summary: The research demonstrates a method using molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) to create single T centres in silicon-on-insulator wafers. This epitaxial approach significantly improves the coherence of photon emission from these defects by narrowing the optical linewidth down to 30 MHz. These results establish a highly promising, scalable platform for developing quantum photonic devices.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving coherent photon emission from spin-photon interfaces based on silicon quantum emitters for scalable quantum computing.
main_result: Epitaxially incorporating single T centres in silicon-on-insulator yields significantly narrower optical linewidths (as low as 30 MHz) compared to standard ion-implanted samples, establishing a robust platform for coherent spin-photon interfaces.
method: The authors utilized high-purity molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) to grow and incorporate single T centres into SOI wafers, followed by advanced optical characterization techniques like hole-burning and second-order correlation measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is a single T centre defect engineered epitaxially within silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers, coupled to nanophotonic waveguides. The T centre acts as the quantum emitter whose spin state couples to emitted photons.
key_observables: Optical linewidths (homogeneous: 30 MHz vs. hundreds of MHz for implanted), single-photon emission confirmation ($g^{(2)}(0) = 0.26(3)$), and spectral diffusion decay times ($\sim 34 \mu	ext{s}$).
important_parameters: The epitaxial process involves specific MBE growth steps (e.g., $\delta$-doping, low-temperature deposition) to achieve nanometer-scale defect control.
main_assumptions: It is assumed that the tailored MBE process successfully mitigates material imperfections responsible for spectral wandering and homogeneous broadening compared to implantation methods.
figures_summary: Figures compare PL spectra (ensemble vs. single emitter), show $g^{(2)}(\Delta t)$ measurements confirming single-photon emission, and present hole-burning results comparing linewidths between epitaxial and implanted samples.
paper_structure: The paper details the MBE growth process for T centres in SOI, presents characterization using PL and $g^{(2)}$ measurements to confirm single emitters, and critically compares the resulting optical coherence properties (linewidths) against previously achieved ion-implanted samples.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of creating high-quality quantum light sources on CMOS-compatible silicon platforms by controlling material defects epitaxially, which is central to solid-state quantum networking and computing architectures.
